Oct 27 : Fenerbahce condemned a brawl that broke out on the pitch after their 2-1 derby defeat by Galatasaray in the Turkish Super Lig on Monday. Players and staff from both teams rushed onto the field after a scuffle between Fenerbahce's Kerem Akturkoglu and Galatasaray's Roland Sallai, according to video shared on social media. "The rivalry and tension of the derby do not give anyone the right to attack our players," Fenerbahce said in a statement. "What happened cannot be dismissed as 'derby tension.' The behaviour of the opposing team's members, instead of reducing tension, fuelled the incidents." Fenerbahce have called for an investigation and disciplinary action against those responsible for the brawl.

Oct 27 : Sri Lanka reached the final of the one-day international Tri-series in Pakistan with a comfortable eight-wicket victory over the hosts in Lahore on Tuesday. The result ensured England, who lost their first three matches, were knocked out of the tournament with a game to spare.  Pakistan were dismissed for 110, Sri Lanka's left-arm seamer Dilshan Madushanka starred with the ball, claiming a career-best 5-34 to earn the player-of-the-match award. "We had a plan and followed it. Because of that, as a team, we were able to bowl them out for a low score," Madushanka said.

Oct 27 : Super Micro-backed cloud computing firm Argentum AI is in talks to secure a $5 billion financing deal for AI chips with a major private credit firm, according to two people familiar with the matter.  One of the people said the money would pay for additional chips for the data center Argentum secured in Poland with DL Invest Group, and that the debt is meant for chips leased to customers that do not have investment-grade ratings. Argentum has secured more than $12 billion in contracted revenue, the person said. The deal comes as financing for neoclouds, which rent out AI computing power to other companies, has tightened.

Elon Musk wrote on X on Sunday that debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for companies without substantial revenue independent of AI data centers. He predicted that 200-plus neoclouds will see "guppy-level death and consolidation." SpaceX secured $40 billion of debt for chips with an affiliate of Apollo Global Management on Monday. Musk credited the rockets-to-AI firm's investment-grade rating and its Starlink and launch revenue. AI cloud services firm Nebius last week secured a $3.5 billion financing facility from Citi to fund the continued development of its data centers and GPU purchases as it races to expand capacity. Argentum, led by founder and CEO Andrew Sobko, is an independent, institutional-grade AI cloud platform focused on deploying large-scale GPU infrastructure for enterprise AI. The Chicago-based startup was founded in 2025. The startup signed a roughly $2.5 billion deal in May with cloud gaming firm Boosteroid and DL Invest for a 300-megawatt data center. The company had said then that it was working with US financial institutions and investment banks on financing structures for future deployments.

HEBRON, West Bank: Israeli troops fired a stun grenade on Tuesday (Oct 27) to disperse Palestinians who gathered to protest against an Israeli military operation that has displaced thousands of residents from a neighbourhood in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. The unrest, which follows the deaths of two Israeli soldiers shot by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week, unfolded as Israelis were voting in an election in which the country's posture in the West Bank has been a major political issue. Some Palestinian officials have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of launching a crackdown in the West Bank to coincide with the vote, as a way to energise his right-wing supporters. The government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers. A group of Palestinian men, women and children gathered at Tuesday's protest. One elderly man held a placard that said: "No to collective punishment, no to closures, and no to displacement."

The military said it had fired a stun grenade to disperse them so that its operation could continue.

A Palestinian man holds a placard which reads: "No to collective punishment / No to closure and no to displacement" during a protest in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Oct 27, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Mussa Qawasma)

On Monday, the United Nations said that over 3,000 Palestinians had been forced from their homes by the Israeli military operation, which targeted neighborhoods near the checkpoint where Palestinian gunmen killed the two Israeli soldiers on Friday. "Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," said UN human rights chief Volker Türk in a statement. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing." The Israeli military said in a statement on Sunday that troops would carry out demolitions in the area. It said soldiers had not located any weapons in searches of the houses. Since Friday's attack on the checkpoint, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns across the West Bank, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement. Noura Nassar, a displaced resident who attended the protests, said she had struggled to get medical treatment because of the blockages. "Where is the democracy in all of this? Their elections are today, sure, but what about us? Aren't we human beings? We want to go out, we want to visit the doctor," said Nassar.

A child looks at a banner depicting Israeli Prime Minister and Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu, during the country's national elections in Jerusalem, Oct 27, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Ronen Zvulun)

Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot both oppose the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. Residents expelled from the Hebron neighbourhood said Tuesday's election in Israel would do little to change the reality on the ground in territories Israel has occupied since 1967. "Among themselves they will elect who is the oppressor and who will destroy the Palestinian people. That is their election," said Sana' Salman Abu Sneineh, another expelled resident. Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements, which are deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Under Netanyahu's right-wing coalition there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians.

FAST

LONDON, Oct 27 : Four years ago, Alexia Putellas appeared untouchable, the dazzling Barcelona captain who became the first woman to win back-to-back Ballon d'Or Feminin awards. Then came a devastating knee injury, months of rehabilitation and an uncomfortable question: had the world's best player already enjoyed her peak? On Monday night, the answer was emphatic. The Spanish midfielder reclaimed women's football's highest individual honour, winning a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or Feminin and joining compatriot Aitana Bonmatí as the only players to lift the trophy three times.

"All the boys and girls around the world, if you love football and if you want to play football, play football," she said in her acceptance speech. "It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl. Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself." For many players, the award would represent a crowning achievement. For 32-year-old Putellas, it felt more like a full-circle moment. By the summer of 2022, she had established herself as the outstanding player in women's football, winning consecutive Ballon d'Or awards and leading Barcelona to the top of the European game, having won their first Champions League title in 2021. Then everything came to a halt. Days before Spain began their European Championship campaign, Putellas suffered a ruptured ACL, an injury that not only cost her the tournament but also threatened to alter the trajectory of her career. Rehabilitation kept her out for almost a year and returning did not immediately mean returning to her best. She arrived at the 2023 Women's World Cup still searching for full fitness and later underwent further knee surgery after another setback. REBUILD For perhaps the first time in her career, Putellas was forced to chase the standards she had once set herself. As Barcelona continued to collect silverware and new names emerged, the spotlight shifted elsewhere. Rather than accepting a supporting role, she rebuilt. Gradually the sharpness returned, then the confidence and, eventually, the influence that had made her the game's dominant player. Last season was the clearest evidence yet. Putellas won her 10th Liga F title with Barcelona, in addition to her 10th Copa de la Reina, and fourth Champions League crown, scoring 20 goals in all competitions. She moved to Women's Super League side London City Lionesses in July after 14 years at Barca, embracing the challenge of leading owner Michele Kang's insurgent outfit to disrupt the established order in England's top flight. Putellas has also used her profile to help bring the women's game to new audiences, most notably through the launch of her YouTube channel, ElevenTV. The platform acquired rights to show WSL matches in Spain. Monday's award was about more than another outstanding season. It was recognition of a journey back from the most serious challenge of her career and confirmation that one of the defining players of the modern era had reclaimed her place at the top.

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU, Oct 27 : High inflation will persist in the global economy well into next year, according to hundreds of economists polled by Reuters, who are now increasingly concerned that price pressures will become entrenched beyond rising energy costs caused by the conflict in the Middle East. More than $1 trillion of investment in artificial intelligence technology globally since last year has made some economies more resilient at a time when cost of living pressures are squeezing households and shaping national politics. Most central banks have raised interest rates only a few times or not at all, but more could come if inflation pressures broaden. A global rout in bond markets in recent months has also tightened financial conditions through higher yields. Crude oil prices, which have stayed above $100 a barrel since October 7, hit a six-month high of over $117 last week and are up more than 60 per cent since the US-Israeli war with Iran began almost eight months ago.

Even forecasters who did not anticipate a quick end to the war are now sounding more concerned about inflation resurgence, particularly given the resilience of global growth. More than 500 economists Reuters surveyed globally this month raised their 2027 inflation forecasts for 31 of the 50 economies polled on and growth forecasts for 23 of them. "I am getting much more concerned about inflation again," said Janet Henry, global chief economist at HSBC. "The longer the situation evolves and escalates in the Middle East and the higher the broad basket of price pressures builds, the greater the likelihood that we get not just higher but more persistent inflation." Economists raised 2027 inflation forecasts for 15 of 21 developed economies covered. That suggests inflation worries are spreading and affecting economies that typically experience low price pressures. Cumulatively, median forecasts for 2027 inflation over the past three quarterly polls have risen by 0.7 per centage points for Britain, 0.5 per centage points for the euro zone and only 0.2 per centage points so far for the US. They have risen by 0.4 per centage points for India and by 0.5 per centage point for Brazil. "Higher energy prices continue to ripple through the global economy, but economic activity remains resilient, supported by the AI-led investment cycle and firmer-than-expected activity across several regions," Seth Carpenter, global chief economist at Morgan Stanley, said in a note. "The inflation picture has become more complex as signs of energy pass-through into core measures are beginning to emerge." The effects of rising prices on household budgets have taken centre stage in various political campaigns across the world. Opinion polls show voters ahead of US midterm elections on November 3 are preoccupied with these issues and Brazil's presidential election, which gave incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva his fourth non-consecutive term, was also fought on cost of living issues. In contrast to two previous polls in April and July, which painted a weak-growth, high-inflation scenario, the latest forecasts lean towards one where price pressures accompany more robust economic performance. Economists upgraded their global growth forecasts for both this year and next, to 3.0 per cent and 3.2 per cent, respectively, from 2.9 per cent and 3.1 per cent in the July poll, though the 2027 forecast is lower than the 3.4 per cent the International Monetary Fund is predicting. The US, which leads in AI capital expenditure that has now become the main driver of domestic growth, is forecast to expand 2.3 per cent this year and 2.1 per cent in 2027. SEATTLE, Oct 27 : Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on Tuesday that the company will not reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month until early 2027, a serious setback to the company's ongoing recovery. As a result, the company will not hit its delivery target of 500 jets this year. The company also expects much slower free cash flow growth than investors had expected - $3 billion next year and $6 billion in 2028, compared to Wall Street analysts' consensus projection of $5.6 billion and $9.6 billion, respectively, according to LSEG data. Shares of the US planemaker fell 9.5 per cent in early trading, reaching April 2025 lows, even as Boeing continues to recover from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load. The company had planned to reach 47 737 jets per month this past summer, but it will take "into early next year," Ortberg said during an interview on CNBC.

In September, he said that Boeing has not been able to make wings fast enough. Deliveries of the popular single-aisle jetliner are a major driver of Boeing's cash flow. "We are ramping up aircraft, and we're doing that in the right way," he said. Before Ortberg joined Boeing in 2024, the company had struggled for years with production quality problems that were attributed to rushing rate increases at the expense of quality. There is pressure on the company to increase 737 output faster, "but we're going to be smart about this, stay disciplined, and the outlook is there," Ortberg said. The company continues to struggle with production challenges in its 787 program and 777 freighters, as first reported by Reuters on Friday. High fuel prices have kept demand up for more fuel-efficient jetliners, but "certainly something we have to continue to watch," Ortberg said on CNBC. During the quarter, Boeing secured certification for the 737 MAX 7 from US regulators, won the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract and generated free cash flow for another quarter, while certification of the larger MAX 10 followed in October. "Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day," Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results. Boeing reported an adjusted loss of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with market expectation of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG. Revenue at Boeing Commercial Airplanes dipped slightly to $10.7 billion, while operating loss stood at $697 million and margin shrank by just 6.5 per cent compared with a contraction of 48.3 per cent a year ago. The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain. At Boeing's defense division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a $252-million sale of a subsidiary contributed to nearly $500 million in quarterly earnings with an operating margin of 6.2 per cent, up from 1.7 per cent a year ago. Boeing Global Services earned $1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3 per cent. The US planemaker ended the quarter with $25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from $25.9 billion in the previous three months and $30.4 billion a year ago.

MANCHESTER, England, Oct 27 : Michael Carrick remained in charge of Manchester United on Tuesday and led training at Carrington, giving the under-pressure manager and his players another opportunity to revive a season that has drifted alarmingly off course. Carrick's future had appeared in serious doubt after Sunday's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth extended United's winless run to eight matches in all competitions and left them hovering one point above the Premier League relegation zone in 16th place. Senior club officials held talks on Monday amid mounting speculation over Carrick's position, with potential replacements already being linked to the job by British media reports. However, no decision was announced and the former United midfielder reported for work as normal, overseeing preparations for Saturday's league trip to Chelsea.

A club source said Carrick and his players will have the opportunity to turn the situation around, with the club focused on preparing for Saturday and showing a response on the pitch. Amid Sunday's frustration at Old Trafford, supporters levelled their anger at the players rather than the manager. As Carrick made his way towards the tunnel after the final whistle, thousands of fans sang his name and applauded him. The mood shifted seconds later when cheers turned to angry boos as the players made their way off the pitch. The scene was a reflection of the goodwill the 45-year-old Carrick still enjoys among a fanbase that remembers both his decorated 12-year playing career at United and the measured manner in which he has carried himself. He has repeatedly accepted responsibility for the team's struggles while shielding his players from scrutiny. "I totally understand the situation," he said after Sunday's loss. "I'm not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I'm carrying on as normal, and I love this place. "I always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club, whatever decision is made on anything really." Carrick turned around United's season when he replaced Ruben Amorim in January, guiding them to third in the league, but they have not won in the top flight this season since they beat newly promoted Ipswich Town on August 30. The pressure on Carrick was intensified last week by his decision to leave captain Bruno Fernandes on the bench four days after the Portugal midfielder publicly criticised United's tactics following a 4-1 Champions League loss at Como. Fans have also aimed their anger at the club's hierarchy in part-owner Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox. United face a tough string of games in fifth-placed Chelsea, followed by AS Roma (Champions League), Aston Villa and Liverpool. Carrick is United's seventh permanent manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann have featured prominently on the list of potential replacements.

NEW DELHI, Oct 27 : India plans to amend its anti-doping law to make peddling banned substances a crime, Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya said on Tuesday, in a potential boost to the country's bid to host the 2036 Olympic Games in Ahmedabad. India has topped the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of offenders for three consecutive years, underscoring the scale of the challenge facing the world's most populous nation. Speaking at a UNESCO anti-doping conference in New Delhi, Mandaviya stressed the ministry's zero tolerance towards "the menace of doping". "India firmly believes that sporting excellence must always be accompanied by integrity," he said.

India also ranked among the top two nations for athletics' anti-doping rule violations between 2022 and 2025. That prompted the Athletics Integrity Unit board to move the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) from Category B to Category A.  Category A federations, deemed the highest risk, face stricter obligations, including minimum testing thresholds for national-team athletes. Local administrators often attribute the high number of cases to increased testing, but doping remains rampant due to easy availability of banned substances, inadequate safeguards and limited athlete awareness.  India's National Anti-Doping Agency conducted more than 7,000 tests and held over 350 awareness sessions for 27,000 athletes in the last two years, Mandaviya added.
